h1: Building Trust With Your Little One
before: Say a friend sits with you while you fall apart. Most of us feel better and call them again the next time, and they get a little better at it every time while we don't. So steal some of it. Usually what helped was how they just sat there without trying to fix you. Ten seconds of sitting with yourself like that is good enough for a start, so try it before you call next time.
fixed_first: It's two in the morning, your little one is lonely, and the ex who dumped you by text is one text away. The Protector is the one who puts the phone in the other room, and in the morning, "I'm glad you're here" is a lot easier for your little one to believe.
after: The next section, "Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust", is about loving your little one before they trust you. It introduces their line "Big fuckity whoopty doo. I don't believe you." Don't use that line or "big whoop" here.
established:
- "Your little one" is the inner child. Never "the kid".
- One grown-up does three jobs: the Nurturer, the Protector and the Guide. Earlier the article showed them in one scene: a party gets too much for your little one, the Protector gets you both out of there, and on the way home the Nurturer tells them they did great, even though mostly they hid in the bathroom.
- The Nurturer sometimes shows up just to say "I'm glad you're here" and enjoy them for a minute.
- Just before this section: borrow from a friend who sat with you while you fell apart; ten seconds of sitting with yourself like that is a start.
plan:
After the first paragraph (fixed), in this order unless the sense needs otherwise. Bare points, not sentences to copy:
A. Ordinary outside acts: set one boundary; say no to something costly; deal with an avoided task or a money mess; leave a relationship that keeps wearing down your safety; keep one small promise; clean your room. Acts like these add up to trust, because soothing without follow-through sounds like the same unreliability that hurt your little one in the first place. The inside half of the job: keeping a surge of fear, rage, craving or shame from running what you say, send, spend or take, or who you sleep with or commit to (the guide's words: "preventing a surge ... from controlling speech, messages, spending, substances, sex, or relationship decisions").
B. Some protective acts happen inside, between you and your little one: hearing their sarcasm without snapping back, letting them distrust you without demanding reassurance, admitting a complaint of theirs is true, repairing after you attack yourself. Your little one sees these as clearly as a clean room or a kept appointment. Not retaliating is evidence of love; it doesn't replace love.
C. When the Nurturer isn't available yet, the Protector can start the relationship. Care may first look like a locked door, a meal, a cancelled obligation. Warmth can come later.
D. Pick one act and make it specific: when, how small the first step can be, what help or resources it needs. A short rehearsal can help with a predictable hard moment. Afterward look at what actually happened. If you didn't do it, don't decide why without looking (fear, not being sure it's the right goal, not knowing how, exhaustion, a practical obstacle). Doing it without feeling relief isn't failure, and doing it doesn't prove it helped. Keep the acts that make things safer, more connected, more capable or more enjoyable, not the ones that just earn a tick. (D can be one or two paragraphs.)
limits:
- Don't invent facts about the author's life, and don't use first person for him unless it's an opinion the points above give.
- Don't reuse the first paragraph's phone or the party scene.
- Keep the points; you can merge, split or reorder clauses, drop a listed example if the sentence gets too long, and add an example of your own only if it's ordinary and true to life.
